prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single B027 part crediting Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Having read the full round-1 exchange, I find the case rests on the content of the discovery and not on the six-way opening agreement, and the chair is right that unanimity can hide different readings of what is honoured. My reading is explicit: the prize recognises how GLP-1 works and what the active molecule is (incretin physiology and GLP-1 secretion, the identification of the biologically active peptide forms, and receptor biology with the route to therapy). That discovery chain has been tested for decades, confirmed in large independent randomized trials, and now extends beyond glycaemia to weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. There is no maturity concern. A single-achievement prize also keeps the three seats for the people most tied to one coherent discovery, and I see no second part whose merit justifies diluting them.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the real weakness. Four credited people compete for three seats, and Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's engineering of long-acting analogues is what turned the biology into the medicines patients actually use. A physiology citation can be read as honouring the hormone and not the drug. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide relative to Joel Habener, who is outside the supplied credit list, is flagged by every member and, as far as I can see, cannot be settled from the material we were given. I will not treat it as resolved. There is also a risk that the committee is carried by the public prominence of semaglutide and tirzepatide, which is not the same as the originality of the underlying discovery. For the fallbacks, CAR-T (B025) has the Eshhar concept outside its credited names and three strands that are distinct achievements, and optogenetics (B035) cannot be cut to three names without excluding someone with a documented claim.

responses.point: The chair asks whether B027 honours GLP-1 physiology and molecular identity (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or incretin-based therapy (bringing Knudsen into the third seat), notes that his own opening trio included Knudsen, and asks what evidence could settle Mojsov's priority.
responses.response: I choose the physiology and molecular identity reading, and I want the citation to say so plainly, so that the Knudsen question is answered by the wording and not left to be inferred. I accept your point that your move from Knudsen to Mojsov followed discussion and is not independent confirmation; my own position did not change between opening and round 1, so I cannot claim to have been persuaded either way. On evidence, nothing in the materials supplied to me can settle the Mojsov-Habener question, so I would not use it to swap in Knudsen. Replacing Mojsov would remove the only named contributor for the identity of the active peptide, which is the part of the discovery that made rational design possible. If the committee found the priority question disqualifying for Mojsov, the right response would be to re-examine the identity part of the citation, not to quietly turn the prize into one for analogue engineering.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks cGAS-STING and orexin ahead of CAR-T, treats the missing earlier chimeric-receptor credit as a real obstacle, and argues that efficacy is still confined to haematological cancers.
responses.response: Your objection to B025 is stronger than I weighted it in round 1. I had treated the Eshhar gap as a limitation, but your point that costimulation, clinical translation and adoptive transfer are distinct strands, not one discovery, is a scientific problem with the unit of the prize and not only a naming problem. That moves B025 closer to a later-year candidate for me, though I keep it as an alternative because its clinical record is the best documented outside B027. Where I still differ is on cGAS-STING. The mechanism is clear and Chen and Barber is a clean pairing, but the pending therapeutic validation and the unresolved Ishikawa, Sun and Wu questions make it a good candidate for a coming year and not a replacement for a mature, validated discovery now.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius proposes Hall alone for TOR as the cleanest attribution and names B025 as the strongest fallback if B027 attribution cannot be defended.
responses.response: I agree that B025 is a sensible fallback if B027 were set aside, with the Eshhar problem you raise still attached to it. I would not set B027 aside, though, because its credit difficulty is about a fourth seat and a priority dispute, not about whether the discovery is real or unified. On Hall alone for TOR, I still think a one-name prize would cut the rapamycin-target and mammalian mTOR chain that carries the medical relevance, so I would treat B011 as a strong candidate whose credit does not fit comfortably into this year's configuration, not as a case for a narrower prize.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks optogenetics second for its causal, millisecond-precision control of circuits, and also records the risk of rewarding clinical and commercial visibility over the originality of the discovery.
responses.response: I share your caution about visibility and take it as a reason to keep the B027 citation on the discovery and not on the drugs. On B035 I agree it is the discovery with the largest effect on research practice, and I ranked it high for that reason. Our difference is whether a transformative tool should lead a physiological discovery with measured patient benefit. I do not think it should this year. I also cannot construct a three-name subset of Nagel, Hegemann, Deisseroth, Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenboeck that I would call free of a defensible objection, and that is why it stays an alternative for me.

responses.point: Sandberg emphasises conceptual clarity and clean credit and ranks cGAS-STING and the unfolded protein response ahead of CAR-T, worrying that an exceptionally visible clinical story could crowd out older, cleaner mechanistic discoveries.
responses.response: I take the worry seriously. The Walter and Mori credit for the unfolded protein response and the Chen and Barber credit for cGAS-STING are cleaner than the B027 credit, and I do not dismiss them. But clean credit alone is not what separates them from B027 for me: B027 has both an original mechanism and verified patient benefit, so placing it above mechanism-only candidates does not reward visibility at the expense of originality. On the second-part question, I considered whether either of your candidates would justify reducing the B027 trio, and I conclude that neither does this year.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide relative to Habener can be established, which I cannot verify from the supplied material.
Whether the committee accepts a citation limited to physiology and molecular identity, or whether the absence of Knudsen will be seen as a defect in a prize that is justified partly by therapy.
Whether CAR-T or optogenetics would become strong enough to justify a second part if a clean three-name credit could be defended; I do not believe either is there now.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name is apparent from my profile. My single-cell and spatial-transcriptomics work, including the 2016 spatial-transcriptomics paper, and eight recorded co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg involve no shortlisted candidate, and I infer no personal ties from shared institutions. This is unchanged from round 1, and no recusal is requested.
